source_document.body:
Container spot rates from Asia to the United States are easing after months of elevated pricing . SONAR data contributor Freightos (NASDAQ: CRGO ) showed Asia–U.S. West Coast prices down 6% this past week to $7,985 per forty-foot container. Asia–U.S. East Coast prices held level at $9,854 per FEU.
Port employers and the International Longshore and Warehouse Union Local 26 watchmen reached a last-minute agreement Nov. 22. It averts disruption at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, but the deal is tentative until ratification. The union will keep working under its expired contract until it votes.
Daily West Coast rates are down to about $7,500/FEU so far this week. That is their lowest level since the end of August. East Coast prices have slid to about $9,000/FEU, back to July levels. Rates remain nearly three times higher than a year ago.
Several factors drove stronger-than-expected trans-Pacific volumes and an extended peak season. These included expectations of tariff increases, while weather-driven congestion and capacity reductions also helped keep rates higher even as demand cooled. Carriers are now adding blanked sailings as volumes soften and, with pre-Lunar New Year demand only a few weeks away, prices are likely to be quite elevated when they start climbing again.
Last week’s Trump-Xi summit ended with calls for stability in the trade relationship. China has since taken further conciliatory steps, including suspending some critical-material export curbs to the U.S. until January. Both sides are still preparing options ahead of the Jan. 10 trade truce expiration.
The Trump administration is planning to raise tariffs on goods from China by an additional 20% and hike import taxes on imports from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners. The proposals come ahead of the findings in a probe into excess manufacturing capacity expected as early as next week.
Several of the targeted countries have rejected the accusations. Freightos said the new tariffs would likely only restore duties to International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) levels, which the U.S. and its partners agreed to last year. It is unclear whether some countries will see that as escalation and retaliate.
Procedural steps would delay any new tariffs, and a comment period and hearings would likely take a couple more months. In the most recent Section 301 case, on forced labor, Trump enacted tariffs eight weeks after the USTR released its report.
Asia–North Europe prices dipped 1% last week to $3,374 per FEU. They have since climbed about $200 to $3,500 as carrier general rate increases push rates up despite a post-peak, pre-Lunar New Year lull. Asia–Mediterranean prices surged 20% to $5,162. Daily rates are up another $300 this week, though prices could backslide in the near term.
When Lunar New Year demand picks up, some forwarders expect existing congestion in North Europe to worsen. That would add upward pressure on rates, Freightos said. It could also lead carriers to start rolling — delaying or shifting — some contracted volumes again.
Why it matters: Falling trans-Pacific rates offer some relief post-holiday, but they are still nearly triple last year’s levels. Blanked sailings, Lunar New Year demand and the Jan. 10 trade truce expiration could push costs back up quickly.
